Watch for butterflies! This is likely peak week for the monarch migration from the Lake Erie islands to northwest Ohio.

There is indeed still enormous amounts (albeit much less than previously) of monarchs gathering in the waning days of summer. Point Pelee is the last land mass on their journey across Lake Erie.
Based on the foliage in this photo, it’s more likely to have been taken in a Mexican wintering locale.
Asclepias tuberosa or butterfly milkweed. Always a favorite for butterflies. #nativeplants #greatlakes #indinadunes #manisteenationalforest
The monarchs decided to stop at the Rose Park on their way up to Lake Erie! Definitely recommend going if you can, there are tons!!

Found this Monarch and two Mourning Cloaks after a storm, exhausted, on the shore of Lake Michigan, wave after wave rolling them in the sand. Helped the others to higher ground, then this one clung to my fingertips for half an hour, 'til I found a nice mullein leaf for it.
#Butterflies #LakeMichigan

When Monarch butterflies cross Lake Superior during their yearly migration, they veer off course to avoid mountains that no longer exist. So ingrained in them is this routine that their distant offspring, tens of thousands of years later, still perform this behaviour.

Thank you, Emily! The Monarch #butterfly migration has been an inspiration to me ever since a kaleidoscope of migrating Monarchs landed in my family's yard during a storm system over Lake Michigan. They stayed for 3 days. Such a marvel of evolution 🦋
#HabitatRestoration #PlantMilkweed
Here are two coats of A Butterfly from Great Lakes Lacquer. Base coat: Essie To The Rescue. Top coat: ORLY Polishield. #nails #nailpolish #manicure

I used to pull out milkweed around the house. Now I've made pollinator gardens with lots of milkweed and the Monarchs arrive every year. One year I caught their migration near Lake Michigan. Thousands of them, fluttering past for hours. One of the most amazing experiences I've seen.

This female monarch took a different route across Lake Erie and crossed from Ontario into Michigan, rather than Ohio like others. LPM086 was released at Birds Canada HQ in Long Point on Sept. 28 at 18:51 UTC, but decided to flutter along the northern coast instead of crossing Lake Erie.
Butterflies migrating across Lake Superior detour around an island that isn't there anymore and hasn't been there in human memory.

Black-fruited sedge, good for butterflies, with coneflower and coreopsis leaves in autumn decline. The garden rock has gouges most likely made while being carried in the Laurentide Ice Sheet, as I pulled it out of a native clay bank on Lake Ontario. #gardening #sedges #gardensky #bloomscrolling
I’m happy to report that last September I watched a steady stream of monarchs flying south along the shore of Lake Michigan.
This beauty is an American Lady (Vanessa virginiensis) butterfly photographed at the end of summer 2024 at Port Burwell Provincial Park in Ontario on the north shore of Lake Erie.
I remember my days in the 70’s where there were endless numbers of Monarchs around the beach of Lake Michigan at my uncle’s cottage

While sitting on the beach at Southwick State Park, NYS, on Lake Ontario on a crystal clear Autumn day a cloud suddenly blocked the sun. I looked up to see thousands of Monarch Butterflies migrating from Canada! It was jaw dropping!
I'm in southern Ontario , Canada near Lake Huron and I've got lots of Monarchs in my yard. Way more than last year., when I had lots of Swallowtails , I've hardly seen any this yr. Lol

North on Pacific butterfly-way we used to see monarchs & swallowtails. Not seen a butterfly in 5 yrs now.😢🦋
I grew up chasing Eastern monarchs. Every autumn we went to Point Pelee Ont to be in the swarm before they crossed Lake Erie. They decimated now too😭
🖕Sixth Extinction ☠️
Don’t think I’ll ever get over the magic of being on a monarch migration path, I’ve seen like 10 this morning coming off Lake Erie, go little buddies go!
These new plants will give monarchs respite during their long migration south, says SWP's Great Lakes Climate Corps crew. Check it out here:
That’s impressive! Almost as much as watching Monarch butterflies launch like fluttering leaves from the shore to cross Lake Erie. Nature can do astounding things.

We have a 50' x 50' garden patch on our property (near Lake Superior), which has dozens of milkweed plants growing in it. We are always eager to witness the migrations, emergence of ravenous caterpillars, their various stages of development, and ultimately their departure, heading north to Canada

filled with what I assumed were Monarchs heading back south. They were way up there. I was in boot camp in Great Lakes, Illinois and my company had just finished lunch and was lining up on the grinder when I looked up and saw this miraculous event. Hard to believe that was just about 45 yrs ago
Get rid of the butterfly bush! It's an invasive species in North America. Here's a planting resource list for attracting Monarch butterflies! List is from xerces.org

There’s a cute little factoid doing the rounds on social media about monarch butterflies apparently knowing of a long gone mountain in Lake Superior but I can’t find any legitimate scientific source for it, only this (interesting but a bit beyond me) paper about their general migration abilities
Lake Ontario and I didn't notice the butterfly until after.

My favorite (only) fact about the great lakes. For years, scientists couldn't figure out why monarch butterflies would fly straight across the Great Lakes for a few dozen miles, go left a few dozen more miles, then back to their regular path. (1/2)

I was blessed to have seen the Monarchs migration …Navy boot camp at Great Lakes in 1980…was mustering on the grinder after lunch and looked up and saw the sky full of these beautiful creatures heading south.
Thanks for the photo…😀😀

I live right on Lake Michigan, at the northern end of the Bay of Green Bay, and during their fall migration they travel right down the western shore of Green Bay. In good years there is a river of monarchs, it's incredible to see.
A migrating Monarch Butterfly (Danaus plexippus) on the shores of Lake Erie. Lake Erie Bluffs Park, Perry Township, Ohio. #butterfly #butterfly #monarchbutterfly #savethebutterflys
Monarchs, my favourite butterfly. 😊 Watching them set off to cross Lake Erie was like seeing courage fly. Tiny, fluttering wings to carry them across a vast body of water is some kind of miracle!
The one time we went, the Monarchs flew early. But I’ll never forget the lonely amazing sight of a single butterfly fluttering off across the vast expanse of Lake Erie.
Point Pelee NP 🇨🇦 (just down the road) publishes a Monarch count daily on their FB page in September. It’s a delight if you can catch 100’s hanging on the trees, waiting to cross Lake Erie 😊

we've a hint of fall for the next few days in toronto, but lots of heat left this year. the monarchs are weeks away here, if there's a wind from the south, they stay in town for a few days building numbers waiting for a wind to help them across lake ontario. native asters and goldenrod are favs.

In 2019, we kayaked on Lake Ontario to watch the airshow, and saw a large number of Monarchs heading over the lake. I thought, wow, maybe what so many of us are doing is helping, but again, last year, I only saw this lonely one in October, and it stayed around my Salvia for hours.

We’ve watched the butterfly migration at Presqu’ile on Lake Ontario, and Long Point and Point Pelee in Ontario.
What an incredible journey.

Hi from the shores of Lake Ontario!
I have a few dozen milkweeds in our garden which seem to attract a lot of fireflies, but no Monarch's yet.

Me either! I knew about Monarch butterflies because they stage out of this park, too… it juts out into the lake, making it a shorter trip across Lake Ontario on the migration route? I mean, not a lot shorter but it’s also an oasis of green in a swath of roads and buildings, so we see everything here

You're correct about the monarch butterfly not being worldwide-well-known but in Canada, where we literally gather to watch them cross the narrowest part of the Great Lakes (they despise water) on their southern migration every autumn, I certainly expected better.
Point Pelee. The monarchs are definitely making a come back. Living at Lake Huron, another place where they mass.

we live waaaay north on the shore of lake superior, and we have a 50 ft X 50 ft garden that has a "milkweed corner" that brings the monarchs to the yard... noting that this past summer their attendance was sparse, so that is GREAT news

I once viewed a tree full of monarchs where they had spent the night during their southern migration. It was on the north shore of Lake Erie. They follow the shoreline to until they can continue their journey south without having to fly over water. Awesome.

Millions of monarchs pass through the park, using it as a staging area before crossing Lake Erie. They gather in large numbers, especially when weather conditions prevent them from immediately crossing the lake.

I used to live near Rondeau Provincial Park on Rondeau Bay ( Lake Erie, Canadian side ). This park was where the Monarchs stopped to rest in September on their way to Mexico. Sometimes, the trees were so loaded with butterflies that they looked like colourful leaves. It was breathtaking. Your pic >>

Since a butterfly is the Bluesky mascot, I thought I would add some pictures of these beautiful insects. This is a Common Buckeye that is widespread in North America. This one was photographed this year on the north shore of Lake Erie.
Nice! We had some Monarchs make it across Lake Erie today.
I was in the UP over the weekend and came across a bunch of milkweed along a walking path next to the shore of Lake Michigan. There were a ton of monarchs. 🦋

Happy National Learn About Butterflies Day🦋 Monarch butterflies are one of the most iconic species in the Great Lakes region! Due to habitat loss, they’re sadly declining in population. Join the NWF Action Fund .bsky.social to help! support.nwfactionfund.org/page/94894/a...

These Monarch catterpillars have to beef up in the next three to six weeks to:
1) make a chrysalis out of their own skin
2) métamorphose into a winged cathedral window
3) fly straight accross lake Ontario all the way down to Mexico 4) reproduce on top of a Mexican fir tree

That reminds me, hey science guy; is it true that monarch butterflies take a dangerous detour over lake superior to avoid a mountain that no longer exists because they inherited a migration pattern and their fleeting flesh remembers long after the stone itself has worn to dust?
